examples.title: Compare seven observations with a seven-day interval
Show every calendar date, with the zero-fill assumption explicit
examples.sql:
SELECT c.day, o.orders AS recorded_orders,
  coalesce(o.orders, 0) AS orders_if_complete
FROM calendar_days c LEFT JOIN daily_orders o USING(day)
WHERE c.day BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-05' AND DATE '2026-01-11'
ORDER BY c.day;

examples.title: Report only full seven-day windows
examples.sql:
WITH moving AS (
 SELECT day, count(*) OVER w AS days_in_frame,
   round(avg(orders) OVER w, 2) AS daily_average
 FROM complete_days
 WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
) SELECT day, days_in_frame, daily_average FROM moving
WHERE day = DATE '2026-01-11' AND days_in_frame = 7;

sampleSpecs.title: Daily counts with gaps
sampleSpecs.description: January 2 is a recorded zero. January 3, 6, and 7 have no source row; deciding what those gaps mean is part of the lesson.

challenge.title: Find missing dates without confusing them with zero
challenge.prompt: Return day for calendar dates with no source row, across January 1–11. Keep the recorded zero on January 2 out of the result.
challenge.hint: Test the joined source key for NULL before coalescing the count.
challenge.starter: SELECT day FROM complete_days WHERE orders = 0 ORDER BY day;
challenge.solution: SELECT c.day FROM calendar_days c LEFT JOIN daily_orders o USING(day) WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.day;
challenge.success: January 3, 6, and 7 have no source row. A zero-filled calendar cannot by itself tell you which dates were missing.
